title: The Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah
era: The Victory That Looked Like Defeat
teaser: They walked to Makkah unarmed and came home with a treaty that read like a surrender.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A dream, then fourteen hundred unarmed men
layers.content:
In 6 AH the Prophet ﷺ saw himself in a dream entering the sacred sanctuary at Makkah in safety, performing the lesser pilgrimage with his followers, their heads shaved. He told some of the Companions, and they were overjoyed. Most of the Emigrants had not seen Makkah in six years.

He had his clothes washed, mounted his camel al-Qaswa', and left Ibn Umm Maktum in charge of Madinah — some accounts name Numailah al-Laithi instead. He marched out on a Monday at the beginning of Dhul-Qa'dah at the head of fourteen or fifteen hundred Muslims; reports differ on the number. Umm Salamah travelled with him. Bedouins of the area joined; many stayed behind. They carried no weapons except the sheathed swords a traveller takes on the road, because they had not come to fight.

At Dhul-Hulaifah he had the sacrificial animals garlanded and everyone entered the state of ihram. The pilgrim's dress was itself the argument: it was not done in Arabia to attack a man dressed for pilgrimage. He sent a man ahead for news, who returned to say that allied tribes had gathered against him and the road to Makkah was completely blocked. He put it to his Companions, who said they would not fight anyone unless they were kept from the pilgrimage.

Quraysh met and resolved to resist at any cost. Two hundred horsemen under Khalid bin al-Walid were sent to surprise the Muslims at the noon prayer. The rules of the Fear prayer were revealed, and the Muslims had already turned onto a rough rocky track. Khalid rode back with nothing.

At a place called Thaniyatul-Murar the Prophet's camel knelt and would not move. He swore there that he would accept any plan the enemy proposed which revered the sanctity of Allah's House. Then he spurred the camel and it leapt up. They pitched camp at the far edge of al-Hudaybiyah, beside a well that held almost no water. The men reported their thirst. He took an arrow from his quiver and put it into the ditch, and water rose until all of them had drunk their fill.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Envoys
layers.subtitle: Four messengers and one night raid
layers.content:
Budail bin Warqa' al-Khuza'i came first, with men of Khuza'ah, and asked why he had come. The Prophet ﷺ answered that he had no design but to perform the lesser pilgrimage at the Sanctuary. Should Quraysh accept the religion, as others had, they were welcome. Should they stop the Muslims, he would fight them to the last man.

Budail carried it back. Quraysh did not want to hear it. They sent Mikraz bin Hafs, whom the Prophet ﷺ named a treacherous man on sight, and he took back the same message.

Al-Hulais bin Alqamah came next. What he saw in the camp — garlanded animals, men in ihram who had come only to worship — impressed him so much that he warned his own people that if they kept Muhammad from the House of Allah, his alliance with them was finished.

Then Urwah bin Mas'ud ath-Thaqafi came to negotiate. He opened by telling the Prophet ﷺ that he had gathered a mixed crowd and brought them against his own kin to destroy them, and expected to see him deserted the next day. Abu Bakr answered that. While Urwah spoke he took hold of the Prophet's beard, and al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah, standing beside him with a sword at his side, struck the hand with his scabbard and told him not to touch it.

But Urwah had been watching the camp. He went back and told Quraysh: I have been to Chosroes, to Caesar and to the Negus in their kingdoms, and never seen a king among a people as Muhammad is among his Companions. If he performs ablution they will not let the water fall to the ground. They will not abandon him. He offers you a reasonable plan; do as you please.

Younger men of Quraysh had no interest in a reasonable plan. Seventy or eighty came down from Tan'im in the night to start a clash in the camp and light a war. Muhammad bin Maslamah, who commanded the guard, took them all. The Prophet ﷺ freed them. «وَهُوَ الَّذِي كَفَّ أَيْدِيَهُمْ عَنكُمْ وَأَيْدِيَكُمْ عَنْهُمْ بِبَطْنِ مَكَّةَ» — 'He withheld their hands from you and your hands from them in the midst of Makkah.' (48:24)
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Pledge Under the Tree
layers.subtitle: A rumour of murder, then every hand raised
layers.content:
Negotiations produced nothing. The Prophet ﷺ asked Umar to go into Makkah and speak to the nobles of Quraysh on his behalf. Umar excused himself: the enmity of Quraysh toward him was too well known, and he had no influential relatives in the city to shield him. He proposed Uthman bin Affan, who belonged to one of the most powerful families in Makkah.

Uthman went to Abu Sufyan and the other chiefs. He told them the Muslims had come only to visit the Sacred House and worship there, with no intention of fighting, and that after the ceremonies they would depart peacefully. He was also to call them to Islam, and carry glad tidings to the believers still in Makkah, men and women, that the conquest was approaching. Quraysh were inflexible and would not permit the visit. They did offer Uthman a circuit of the Ka'bah for himself, if he wanted. He declined: how could he take that opportunity while the Prophet ﷺ was denied it.

Then he did not come back. The camp waited with fear and anxiety. Foul play was suspected, and the suspicion hardened into a report that Quraysh had killed him.

Under a tree at al-Hudaybiyah the Muslims gave the Prophet ﷺ their hands on a solemn pledge that they would not flee, and a group of them pledged death. The first to give it were Abu Sinan al-Asadi and Salamah bin al-Akwa', who promised three times over: at the beginning, in the middle and at the end. Umar held the Prophet's hand while the men came forward. Ma'qil bin Yasar held a branch out of his way. For the absent man he held out his own hand and said: this is for Uthman.

Every person present pledged. One did not: Jad bin Qais, of the hypocrites. When it was complete Uthman arrived, alive, and gave his own.

«لَقَدْ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ إِذْ يُبَايِعُونَكَ تَحْتَ الشَّجَرَةِ» — 'Indeed Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged to you under the tree.' (48:18)

Quraysh had wanted to know whether these people could be frightened. They now had their answer.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What Was Written
layers.subtitle: Four clauses, and a son in chains
layers.content:
The terms were settled: the Muslims would return now and come back next year. They would not stay more than three days, and would come unarmed but for sheathed swords in bags. War would be suspended for ten years, in which both would live in full security and neither raise the sword. Anyone wishing to join Muhammad ﷺ or enter treaty with him was free to; the same for Quraysh. And any man of Quraysh who went over to Muhammad ﷺ without his guardian's consent would be returned, while any of Muhammad's followers who went to Quraysh would not be.

Ali bin Abi Talib wrote it. He began: in the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Suhail bin Amr said he knew nothing of ar-Rahman and insisted on the customary formula, in Your Name, O Allah. The Muslims grumbled; the Prophet ﷺ agreed. He dictated: this is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed with Suhail bin Amr. Suhail protested again: had we acknowledged you as Allah's Messenger, we would neither have prevented you from the Sacred House nor fought you; write your own name and your father's. The Muslims refused. The Prophet ﷺ erased the words himself and dictated: Muhammad, the son of Abdullah.

Then Suhail's son walked into the camp. Abu Jandal, brutally chained, staggering with exhaustion. The Companions tried to get him released. Suhail said an opportunity had arrived for them to show good faith. The Prophet ﷺ said the treaty was not signed when his son entered the camp. Suhail said the terms had been agreed.

Abu Jandal lamented at the top of his voice: Muslims, am I to be returned to the polytheists that they might turn me from my religion. The Prophet ﷺ told him to be patient and resign himself to the Will of Allah, that Allah would provide a way out for him and the helpless with him, and that a pledge taken in Allah's Name would not be broken. Umar rose and spoke words of open anger, which gave Abu Jandal the chance to take a sword to his father. He spared him, and was led away in chains.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What Was Sent Down, and What Followed
layers.subtitle: Fourteen hundred men became ten thousand
layers.content:
He ordered the animals slaughtered. Nobody moved. He repeated it three times; they were too depressed to obey. Umm Salamah advised him to take the initiative. He slaughtered his animal and had his head shaved, and the men followed with grief in their hearts.

Umar could not hold it in. Are you not the true Messenger of Allah, he asked. Why not, the Prophet ﷺ replied. Are we not in the right and our enemies in the wrong? He said it was so. Then we should not suffer humiliation in our faith. I am the Messenger of Allah, he said, I never disobey Him, and He shall help me. Did you not tell us we would perform the pilgrimage? I never told you we would do so this year. Umar was silenced, and went to Abu Bakr, who told him the same thing.

On the road home the Chapter of Victory came down. «إِنَّا فَتَحْنَا لَكَ فَتْحًا مُبِينًا» — 'Verily, We have given you a manifest victory.' (48:1) He summoned Umar and told him. Umar spent years afterwards fasting, praying, giving charity and freeing slaves in expiation for that hour.

The clause on returning fugitives had looked the worst of them and cost the least. Abu Basir escaped to Madinah and was handed back; on the road he killed one escort and the other fled, and when he returned he knew he would be given up again, so he left for the coast at Seeful-Bahr. Abu Jandal joined him, then others, until a colony sat there intercepting Quraysh caravans. Makkah begged the Prophet ﷺ to cancel the clause. He did, and they came in.

He had come to al-Hudaybiyah with fourteen hundred men. Two years later he set out to liberate Makkah with ten thousand. «لَقَدْ صَدَقَ اللهُ رَسُولَهُ الرُّؤْيَا لَتَدْخُلُنَّ الْمَسْجِدَ الْحَرَامَ» — 'Allah has fulfilled His Messenger's true dream: you shall certainly enter the Sacred Mosque.' (48:27) The dream had been accurate. It was simply about a different year. What they signed as a humiliation is what the Qur'an calls a manifest victory, and the distance between the two readings was nothing but time.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, the chapter on the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah — 'whoever leaves us for them has been removed by Allah'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: How many Muslims went out to al-Hudaybiyah, and how were they armed?

options.text: Three thousand, fully equipped for battle
Fourteen or fifteen hundred by differing reports, carrying only the sheathed swords of travellers
Ten thousand, the number that later took Makkah
Seven hundred, the number who reached Uhud

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Muslims Mobilize
quiz.scholar_reflection: They were dressed for pilgrimage, not for war. That was the whole strategy, and it left them entirely exposed if Quraysh decided to fight.

quiz.prompt: Why was Uthman bin Affan sent into Makkah as envoy rather than Umar?

options.text: He was the eldest of the Companions present
Umar refused any negotiation with Quraysh
Umar had no influential relatives in the city to shield him, and Uthman belonged to one of its most powerful families
He had relatives among the Ansar

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — 'Uthman bin 'Affan is sent as a Messenger to the Quraish
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umar named the problem himself, and named the better man for it. Choosing an envoy Quraysh could not casually kill was a judgement about them, not about courage.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ do when Suhail bin Amr refused to let the document call him the Messenger of Allah?

options.text: He broke off the negotiation
He had Ali refuse and the wording stood
He erased the words himself and dictated 'Muhammad, the son of Abdullah'
He left the page unsigned

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Treaty and its Clauses
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Muslims refused to make the change. He made it with his own hand. Suhail had also struck out the opening formula and been given that too.

quiz.prompt: Under the treaty, what became of a man of Quraysh who came over to the Muslims without his guardian's permission?

options.text: He was returned to Quraysh, while anyone leaving the Muslims for Quraysh was not sent back
He was granted asylum in Madinah
He was returned only if he wished to be
The treaty said nothing about individuals

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the clauses of the treaty
quiz.scholar_reflection: It was the clause the camp found most objectionable, and the one that later emptied Makkah of its Muslims when Quraysh themselves asked for it to be cancelled.

quiz.prompt: What did the Sura revealed on the journey home call this treaty?

options.text: A necessary retreat
A trial for the believers
A manifest victory
A year of waiting

quiz.citation: Quran 48:1, Surah al-Fath; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nothing had been conquered and nothing gained that anyone in the camp could see. The verse names the treaty itself as the victory.

quiz.prompt: Quraysh offered Uthman a private circuit of the Ka'bah. He had not seen it in six years. He refused, because the Prophet ﷺ was denied it. What is that refusal?

options.text: Solidarity worth more than the thing he had travelled for
Refusing to be separated out and used
A private worship is worth nothing if it costs the group its case
He could not have faced the camp on his return

quiz.slider_label: Take what is offered — Refuse on principle
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Uthman's mission to the Quraish
quiz.scholar_reflection: The offer was designed to divide him from the others, and it cost him the one thing he had come for. He was already the man they could not kill; he made himself the man they could not buy.

quiz.prompt: Abu Jandal came into the camp in chains and was sent back to the men who had chained him, because the terms had already been agreed. How do you hold that?

options.text: A promise that bends for the sympathetic case is not a promise
It was a cruelty accepted for the sake of something larger
He was told to be patient because relief was actually coming, and it did
There is no clean way to hold it, and the sources do not pretend otherwise

quiz.slider_label: Keep the treaty — Keep the man
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Return of Abu Jandal
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not argue that it was painless. He said the pledge had been taken in Allah's Name, that they were under no circumstances prepared to break it, and that Allah would make a way out. Within two years Abu Jandal was free on the coast and Quraysh were asking for the clause to be dropped.

quiz.prompt: Umar asked whether they were not on the truth and their enemies in the wrong, and why then they should accept humiliation. He was answered, and stayed disturbed, and later spent years in expiation. What does that sequence show?

options.text: Objecting out loud to your leader is not the same as disloyalty
Being right about the principle and wrong about the moment
Conviction that cannot yet see the reason is still being tested
He asked what the whole camp was thinking and nobody else would say

quiz.slider_label: He was owed an answer — He should have waited
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Muslims' Grief and 'Umar's Expression of That
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was not rebuked for asking. He went to Abu Bakr and got the identical answer, and when the Sura came down he was sent for and told first.

quiz.prompt: He allowed 'Messenger of Allah' to be struck from the page, and the opening formula changed, to get a treaty signed. Where is the line between flexibility and concession?

options.text: What is written on a page does not alter what is true
He conceded the wording and kept every substantive term he needed
The Muslims' refusal shows this was genuinely costly, not a small thing
A man secure in who he is can afford to let others deny it in writing

quiz.slider_label: A dangerous concession — A costless one
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Treaty and its Clauses
quiz.scholar_reflection: He erased it with his own hand because his Companions would not. Nothing in the erasure changed the terms of the ten-year truce or the recognition of the Muslims as a party fit to sign with.

quiz.prompt: Twice as many people entered Islam in the two years of the truce as in all the years of fighting before it. What follows from that?

options.text: The call spread faster when nobody was defending a battle line
Quraysh had been the obstacle, not the argument
Peace was the strategy; the treaty was not a pause in it
Fourteen hundred to ten thousand in two years is the only verdict needed

quiz.slider_label: Won by the sword — Won by the truce
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Impact of the Treaty of Al-Hudaibiyah
quiz.scholar_reflection: Once the fighting stopped, men met and talked, and the author observes that none discussed Islam intelligently without entering it. The treaty's worst-looking year was its most productive.
